title: What a life, isn't it?
author: _TheLastGamer

comments.author: Sencha-Games
comments.body:
Game programmers have spent the past 15 years watching artists write awful, unoptimized code in scripting languages that are so easy and high level a baby could learn them. Were told to stop gatekeeping and that these languages were reducing the barrier to GOOD games being made.

So when the barrier to GOOD visual assets was lowered, artists were chill about it, right?

replies.author: Friendly-Piece-6732
replies.body:
People used to shit on ai code because it was bad. Nowadays its.. well acceptable quality. AI art looks like dogshit, and people will stop saying that when it stops looking like dogshit.

What is more annoying about AI art though is that it forces your game into the AI category and is an objectively braindead business decision in this climate. Paying an artist or selling ownership equity to an artist is just the smart thing to do.

Perhaps many of the shovel buying grifters arent aware of it on a business level but if you actually made anything remotely of quality on a gameplay and code level. you can easily get an artist that will do everything for free.

So either these people do not know you can do that (dumb) or are completely incapable of making something remotely decent for an artist to sign on for equity (dumb).

Either way like everything related to the AI art sphere is dumb and I am sure its more aggravating than just to people like me.

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
My pfp is an example of "hybrid AI art" - art that was drawn by hand by myself, and then refined by AI for smaller details, and then the details painted over again by me for consistency and to noise.  


I wouldn't be surprised if other artists are using hybrid workflows. It is something I will be forced to disclose when my game(s) hit Steam, because I am very public about my AI usage, lol.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
There's that "artist will do everything for free" stuff I keep seeing again and again. Who exactly is going to do that for some unknown devs upcoming game that has no promise of selling? 

And why is it considered acceptable to get actual artists to put in effort for free? I can't afford a few hundred bucks to pay an artist. And I don't feel it's fair to lowball them or promise "my game will sell heaps bro, trust me." How is that going to pay their bills? 

So I generate my art with extensive prompts. The service for that costs me a few bucks a month. The service to convert it to 3d costs a bit more than that. And I have complete creative control.

I don't believe getting artists to offer their work for free is the answer.

comments.author: tomato-shadow
comments.body:
People have always cared about art and visuals in general in games. It's always been a debate ever since video games have existed.

It's not the fact that your art is AI generated. It's the fact that it's an incoherent mess.

People were critical of state of the art graphics back then. People have criticized pixel art, low poly or stylized art as looking bad or not realistic and all of those were made by hand and took a lot of effort.

So how can people expect to be praised when they pump out generic AI generated stuff? No matter how good you personally think it is, if you lack artistic vision, if your art is inconsistent and incoherent... People are gonna criticize it.

And even if it was all great... Art is subjective and not everyone is gonna like it anyway.

It's so easy to complain about "haters" instead of looking at what you're producing and asking yourself how you could improve it or how it compares to over 30 years of amazing hand made art in games. There's a lot of competition. Of course people are going to be drawn to higher effort and higher quality stuff...

comments.author: Progalist
comments.body:
[ Wall of text incoming, which is the cost of nuance :( ]

The first question you should ask is: Who is creating the game? If I use google images for all my art assets and maybe use some editing to make the player's hair blue, did I create the player character asset? If I prompt a freelance artist to draw some backgrounds, and ask them to make some adjustments a few times, did I create those backgrounds myself by the act of prompting them? Throughout history, artists have been confronted multiple with new tools that change or speed up the art process drastically. The act of AI prompting is different, and a little deceptive, since the interactivity of prompting + getting immediate results tricks people into feeling like they are responsible for the output themselves, and it can make them feel incredibly powerful. AI output is generated by seeing common patterns in the existing artworks it was trained on (without consent of the artists). There is a layer of abstraction in those patterns, but aside from that, AI doesn't magically generate new art. It can't come up with something new, and it doesn't have intent in any way (besides replicating existing intent that was already in the training data itself).

Of course it's fine to use free to use assets, or once that you commissioned or paid for. My metaphor from above only applies to AI partly. 

As for programming, the difference is that code and art have a very different purpose. The code is not part of the end result that the user will see, and therefore not part of the created experience. Code is an intermediate tool to make the design of a game concretely playable, and player actions limited to what the devs allow. Unlike boardgames, where the players themselves have access to the whole ruleset, and where it's an active part of the final experience. This changes the whole story of what it means to use AI.

In my experience, programmers are often a lot more open towards use of AI (if used properly and with care). It fits their existing paradigm of automating the repetitive or boring tasks.

AI is a complicated discussion with various uses and gray areas, and that nuance means that comments need to use more text to discuss things fairly. Those longer comments are also ones that easily get buried below the more vocal, flanderized one-liner arguments, becoming a shouting contest like most political arguments.
